item.title: Practical System Preparation Tips for Molecular Dynamics Simulations
item.description:
The trajectory is already biased before the first step. The box decides how much water you pay for. The termini decide whether a fragment carries charges it never had. The frame you pick afterwards decides whether you publish an outlier.

Which box

A cubic box is orthogonal, easy to look at, and easy to debug. For a globular protein it also packs badly: the corners fill with water that the solute never touches. That is a larger system and a higher cost for the same buffer.

A truncated octahedron is closer to a sphere. For spherical solutes it cuts the solvent count by roughly 30 to 40 percent and still wraps the solute in an even shell. It is the usual compromise.

A rhombic dodecahedron leaves the least empty solvent for a given buffer. The shape is less obvious. Current MD codes handle it. The saving matters once the solute is large. This note does not give a percent for that saving.

Box Advantage Limit
Cube Simple, and natural for an elongated solute Least efficient for a globular protein
Truncated octahedron Balance of simplicity and solvent count A less obvious geometry
Rhombic dodecahedron Smallest solvent volume Least intuitive shape

When to cap the termini

A full-length chain has a real N terminus and a real C terminus. A fragment cut out of a domain does not. The cut ends are charged as if they were the ends of the protein, and they are often buried in the parent structure. That charge invents salt bridges, pulls on the fold, and shows up later as “dynamics.”

The usual caps close the backbone. ACE is the acetyl cap on the N terminus. NME is the N-methylamide cap on the C terminus.

Cap a peptide, an isolated domain, or a stretch you extracted from a larger chain. Leave the termini alone on a full-length protein whose natural ends are solvent-exposed and part of the biology.

Which frame represents the ensemble

The frame that has wandered farthest from the start is easy to notice and a poor representative. It can be one excursion.

Pool the runs. Align on a stable reference region. Measure the variation you care about: RMSD, distances between key residues, or the pocket. Cluster. Take the centroids. Those are the conformations the ensemble actually spent time in.

item.title: Ten Critical Pitfalls in Molecular Dynamics Simulations and Strategies for Mitigation
item.description:
The dangerous MD error is the one that finishes. A missing atom, a mixed force field, or a broken periodic image will still give you a plot. The ten items below are the ones that show up as a plausible trajectory rather than as a crash.

1. The PDB is not a starting model

A downloaded structure can miss atoms, leave residues unresolved, or include crystal contacts that are not present in solution. Build missing loops, clear steric clashes, and set protonation for the pH you are simulating. Histidine tautomers are the usual example of a default that is wrong. pdbfixer, H++, and PropKa are the tools named for that cleanup.

2. The force field has to match the molecule

Popularity is a weak reason. A protein force field is not automatically a membrane force field. Mixing parameter sets is worse: CHARMM protein parameters with OPLS ligand parameters do not share one potential. If you do combine sets, they need compatible functional forms and Lennard-Jones combination rules, and the combination needs to have been validated for that class of molecule.

3. The water model was part of the parameterization

TIP3P and a 4-point model such as OPC are not interchangeable add-ons. The force field paper says which water was used. A mismatch moves density, protein–solvent interaction, and diffusion, which is enough to make a thermodynamic property meaningless.

4. Automated ligand parameters are a draft

CGenFF, PRODRG, and MCPB will write a topology. They also approximate charges and bonded terms, and they say so in penalty scores or warnings. Read the log. For a result you will defend, check partial charges against a QM calculation and bonded terms against experiment or a higher level of theory.

5. Production starts after the system has settled

Minimize until the maximum force is below a tight threshold. The example given is 1000 kJ/mol/nm. Then watch NVT and NPT. Density and potential energy need a plateau before you collect data. Starting earlier is a common source of a trajectory that looks unstable for a boring reason.

6. The time step

2 fs is the standard biological step when bonds to hydrogen are constrained with LINCS or SHAKE. A larger step, such as 4 fs, belongs with hydrogen mass repartitioning. A step that is too long integrates badly. A step that is too short mostly wastes time.

7. Periodic images

The box is required. It also splits molecules across the boundary. Radius of gyration ($R_g$) and RMSD on a broken molecule are the wrong numbers. Recenter and unwrap first. gmx trjconv and cpptraj are the usual tools.

8. One trajectory is an anecdote

The integrator is stochastic once the initial velocities are. Run the same system 3 to 5 times with different seeds. A rare event in one run is not a property of the system until the other runs agree.

9. A flat RMSD is a weak stability claim

RMSD says the structure has stopped drifting from the reference you chose. It does not certify local packing, hydrogen bonds, or the energy. Read it with RMSF, $R_g$, SASA, and a clustering of the trajectory.

10. Compare with something measured

A simulation that does not crash can still be the wrong physical system. Crystallographic B-factors, chemical shifts, and NOEs are the experimental contacts named here. Use the observable you actually have. The comparison is what licenses the interpretation.

item.title: A Quick Guide to Temperature Replica Exchange Molecular Dynamics
item.description:
One thermostat at 300 K will sit in the basin where you started. Temperature replica exchange runs copies of the same system on a temperature ladder and swaps neighbors so that a barrier crossed at high temperature can appear in the 300 K ensemble.

The example is eight replicas from 300 K to 370 K, in 10 K steps, exchanging every 1000 steps. The .mdp files are not pasted here. Only the temperatures and the mdrun line are.

Why a ladder

A rugged landscape traps a single 300 K run. A hotter replica crosses barriers more often. Swaps are accepted or rejected so that each temperature still samples the Boltzmann distribution at that temperature. In a protein–ligand system the states you are usually missing are induced fit, an alternate loop, a cryptic pocket, or a folding event. Short dynamics of a small molecule often do not need this.

The acceptance probability

For replicas \( i \) and \( j \), the swap probability \( P \) is the Metropolis form recorded for this method:

P = min(1, exp[(1/Ti - 1/Tj) * (Ej - Ei)])

Ti and Tj are the temperatures. Ei and Ej are the potential energies. Spacing that is too wide kills the acceptance. Spacing that is too tight spends replicas without helping. This note aims at a 20–30% acceptance rate.

Eight GROMACS inputs

Create md_300.mdp through md_370.mdp with the temperature each replica should hold. Then grompp each one. -maxwarn 1 is part of the recorded command.

gmx grompp -f md_300.mdp -o topol_300.tpr -c conf.gro -p topol.top -maxwarn 1
gmx grompp -f md_310.mdp -o topol_310.tpr -c conf.gro -p topol.top -maxwarn 1
gmx grompp -f md_370.mdp -o topol_370.tpr -c conf.gro -p topol.top -maxwarn 1

The middle temperatures follow the same pattern. The run itself:

mpirun -np 8 gmx_mpi mdrun -multi 8 -replex 1000 -s topol_.tpr -deffnm remd

-multi 8 is the eight replicas. -replex 1000 attempts an exchange every 1000 steps. -s topol_.tpr matches the shared prefix of the .tpr files. One rank per replica is the cost model here.

Demux before you analyze

mdrun -replex writes trajectories that follow a rank, not a temperature. Demultiplex, then take the frames that sat at 300 K.

gmx demux -f remd0.xtc -demux replica_index.xvg

Equilibrate every replica before the exchange run. Analyze the lowest temperature. The hotter trajectories are the mechanism that feeds it, not a second ensemble to mix into the same plot.

item.title: Principal Component Analysis and Free Energy Landscape Mapping Using GROMACS
item.description:
A free-energy landscape in this workflow is a histogram of the trajectory in the plane of the first two principal components. PCA finds those axes. SHAM turns the occupancy into a free energy. The frame you extract is only as meaningful as the components you kept.

The trajectory names come from the 100 ns run md_0_100. One projection file is labeled lovastatin (pc15_lovastatina.xvg). That is the example name, not a requirement.

Covariance

gmx covar wants a .tpr. If a run was pointed at md_0_100.gro and failed, use the .tpr. When prompted, select protein and ligand.

gmx covar -s md_0_100.tpr -f md_0_100.xtc -o eigenvalues.xvg -v eigenvectors.trr -xpma covar.xpm

How many components

From eigenvalues.xvg:

  • Total variance is the sum of the eigenvalues.
  • Explained variance of one component is that eigenvalue divided by the total, times 100.
  • Cumulative variance adds those fractions until you pass the cutoff.

Keep the smallest set of components whose cumulative variance is more than 50%.

Project PC1 through PC5

-proj writes a 1D time series for each selected eigenvector. -2d writes a combined projection of the first five. -tu ns puts the time axis in nanoseconds. The lovastatin filenames are the example.

gmx anaeig -f md_0_100.xtc -s md_0_100.tpr -v eigenvectors.trr -first 1 -last 5 \
-proj pc15_lovastatina.xvg -2d project2d_s100_lovastatina.xvg -tu ns

The PC1–PC2 plane

Project the first component, then the second, and paste them into one three-column file. The awk fields assume the usual .xvg layout of this paste: time and value from PC1, then the value from PC2.

gmx anaeig -f md_0_100.xtc -s md_0_100.tpr -v eigenvectors.trr -last 1 -proj pc1.xvg
gmx anaeig -f md_0_100.xtc -s md_0_100.tpr -v eigenvectors.trr -first 2 -last 2 -proj pc2.xvg
paste pc1.xvg pc2.xvg | awk '{print $1, $2, $4}' > PC1PC2.xvg

Free energy with SHAM

gmx sham -f PC1PC2.xvg -ls FES.xpm

xpm2txt.py turns the XPM matrix into three columns: X, Y, and energy. The invocation recorded here is Python 2.7.

python2.7 xpm2txt.py -f FES.xpm -o fel.dat

The minimum

Plot fel.dat, read the time of the lowest point, and dump that frame. The example time is 520 ps. It is not a universal minimum.

gmx trjconv -s md_0_100.tpr -f md_0_100.xtc -o min_energy.pdb -dump 520

That PDB is the conformation that occupied the bottom of this PC1–PC2 histogram. It is not, by itself, proof that the simulation visited every basin that matters. The 50% cutoff and the choice to stop at two components are the assumptions sitting under the picture.

item.title: Step-by-Step MD Simulation of a Protein–Ligand Complex with GROMACS
item.description:
This is a recorded CHARMM36 recipe, not a universal GROMACS map. The protein uses CHARMM36, the ligand uses CGenFF, and the write-up calls the solvent TIP3P. The commands below are the ones to copy. Menu numbers and index groups belong to the system they were answered on.

em.mdp, nvt.mdp, npt.mdp, and md.mdp are not in this note. The production run is the 100 ns job written as md_0_100. Ions use the short ions.mdp that is included.

0. Repair the PDB

Missing atoms get filled before the force field sees the file.

conda activate pdbfixer
pdbfixer protein.pdb --output=protein_fixed.pdb

1. Separate the ligand

Unknown residues and cofactors should not go through pdb2gmx as part of the protein. Two variants are recorded. One pulls UNK only. The other also drops FAD.

grep UNK protein.pdb > unk.pdb
grep -v "UNK" protein.pdb > clean.pdb

grep -v -e "UNK" -e "FAD" protein_fixed.pdb > clean.pdb

conda activate pdbfixer
pdbfixer clean.pdb --output=clean.pdb

2. Protein topology

pdb2gmx is run with -ter and -ignh. The six lines are the menu answers recorded for this CHARMM36 setup. On another GROMACS build the same digit can be a different force field or a different terminus. Read the menu.

gmx pdb2gmx -f clean.pdb -o processed.gro -ter -ignh << EOF
1
1
0
0
0
0
EOF

3. Ligand MOL2

Hydrogens are added and a 3D guess is generated. The sed line sets the residue name to UNK.

obabel unk.pdb -O unk.mol2 --addh --gen3d
sed -i '2s/.*/UNK/; s/UNK1/UNK/g' unk.mol2

4. Bond order in the MOL2

perl sort_mol2_bonds.pl unk.mol2 unk_fix.mol2

5. CGenFF

The binary path is the one used on this machine. The conversion script targets charmm36-jul2022.ff. Penalty scores in the CGenFF log are a reason to stop. This recipe does not inspect them for you.

~/mdrun/silcsbio.2024.1/cgenff/cgenff unk_fix.mol2 -f unk.str
chmod +x cgenff_charmm2gmx.py

conda activate cgenff
python cgenff_charmm2gmx.py UNK unk_fix.mol2 unk.str charmm36-jul2022.ff

rm cgenff_charmm2gmx.py

6. Ligand coordinates as GRO

The next step expects unk_ini.pdb and, when a cofactor is present, fad_ini.pdb. The command that writes those two names is not in this note. The MOL2 above is the file that went to CGenFF.

gmx editconf -f unk_ini.pdb -o unk.gro
gmx editconf -f fad_ini.pdb -o fad.gro

7. Merge into one GRO

Protein plus ligand. The second line of a GRO file is the atom count, so it is rewritten after the append. The box line is dropped from the protein file and a blank box line is added back at the end.

cp processed.gro complex.gro && sed -i '$d' complex.gro && tail -n +3 unk.gro >> complex.gro && echo " " >> complex.gro

num1=$(sed -n '2p' complex.gro)
num2=$(sed -n '2p' unk.gro)
sum=$((num1 + num2))
sed -i "2s/.*/ $sum/" complex.gro

Protein plus FAD plus UNK:

cp processed.gro complex.gro && \
sed -i '$d' complex.gro && \
tail -n +3 fad.gro >> complex.gro && \
tail -n +3 unk.gro >> complex.gro && \
echo " " >> complex.gro

num1=$(sed -n '2p' processed.gro)
num2=$(sed -n '2p' fad.gro)
num3=$(sed -n '2p' unk.gro)
sum=$((num1 + num2 + num3))
sed -i "2s/.*/ $sum/" complex.gro

8. Topology includes

These sed edits are brittle. They assume the CHARMM36 comments and the molecule name Protein_chain_A are still in topol.top. Open the topology after they run.

Ligand only:

sed -i '/; Include Position restraint file/{:a;N;/#endif/!ba;s/\n#endif\n/\n#endif/;s/#endif/#endif\n\n; Include ligand topology\n#include "unk.itp"/}' topol.top

sed -i '/; Include forcefield parameters/{:a;N;/#include ".\/charmm36-jul2022.ff\/forcefield.itp"/!ba;s/#include ".\/charmm36-jul2022.ff\/forcefield.itp"/&\n\n; Include ligand parameters\n#include "unk.prm"/}' topol.top

sed -i '/\[ molecules \]/,/Protein_chain_A/ {/Protein_chain_A/ a\\nUNK 1\n}' topol.top

FAD and UNK:

sed -i '/; Include Position restraint file/{:a;N;/#endif/!ba;s/#endif/#endif\n\n; Include ligand topologies\n#include "fad.itp"\n#include "unk.itp"/}' topol.top

sed -i '/; Include forcefield parameters/{:a;N;/#include ".\/charmm36-jul2022.ff\/forcefield.itp"/!ba;s|#include ".\/charmm36-jul2022.ff\/forcefield.itp"|&\n\n; Include ligand parameters\n#include "fad.prm"\n#include "unk.prm"|}' topol.top

sed -i '/\[ molecules \]/,/Protein_chain_A/ {/Protein_chain_A/ a\\nFAD 1\\nUNK 1\n}' topol.top

9. Box and solvent

The buffer is 1.4 nm and the box is cubic. Solvation is spc216.gro. That is the SPC216 coordinate file, used here with the CHARMM36 topology. It is not rewritten as tip3p.gro.

gmx editconf -f complex.gro -o newbox.gro -bt cubic -c -d 1.4
gmx solvate -cp newbox.gro -cs spc216.gro -p topol.top -o solv.gro

10. Ions

The ion .mdp is only a steep minimizer so genion has a .tpr. Neutralize, then add 0.15 M NaCl. The heredoc answers group 15. On this system that was solvent. genion prints the group list. Choose solvent, whatever number it has.

cat <<EOF > ions.mdp
integrator = steep
emtol = 1000.0
nsteps = 50000
cutoff-scheme = Verlet
coulombtype = PME
rcoulomb = 1.0
rvdw = 1.0
constraints = none
EOF

gmx grompp -f ions.mdp -c solv.gro -p topol.top -o ions.tpr -maxwarn 3
gmx genion -s ions.tpr -o solv_ions.gro -p topol.top -pname NA -nname CL -neutral -conc 0.15 <<EOF
15
EOF

11. Energy minimization

em.mdp itself is not listed.

gmx grompp -f em.mdp -c solv_ions.gro -p topol.top -o em.tpr
gmx mdrun -v -deffnm em

12. Ligand position restraints

Non-hydrogen atoms of the ligand are restrained with -fc 1000 1000 1000. Group 3 is the selection recorded after 0 & ! a H*. Check the index make_ndx prints.

gmx make_ndx -f unk.gro -o index_unk.ndx << EOF
0 & ! a H*
q
EOF

gmx genrestr -f unk.gro -n index_unk.ndx -o posre_unk.itp -fc 1000 1000 1000 <<EOF
3
EOF

sed -i '/; Include water topology/{x;s/.*/\n; Ligand position restraints\n#ifdef POSRES\n#include "posre_unk.itp"\n#endif\n/;G}' topol.top

13. Complex index

1 | 13 unions two groups that were protein and ligand on this system. Use the numbers your own index file prints.

gmx make_ndx -f solv_ions.gro -o index.ndx << EOF
1 | 13
q
EOF

14. NVT

Temperature equilibration at 300 K, with position restraints. The thermostat settings live in nvt.mdp, which is not pasted here.

gmx grompp -f nvt.mdp -c solv_ions.gro -r solv_ions.gro -p topol.top -n index.ndx -o nvt.tpr
gmx mdrun -deffnm nvt

15. NPT

Pressure equilibration at 1 bar with the Parrinello–Rahman barostat.

gmx grompp -f npt.mdp -c nvt.gro -t nvt.cpt -r nvt.gro -p topol.top -n index.ndx -o npt.tpr
gmx mdrun -deffnm npt

16. Production

The file names are the 100 ns run.

gmx grompp -f md.mdp -c npt.gro -t npt.cpt -p topol.top -n index.ndx -o md_0_100.tpr
gmx mdrun -deffnm md_0_100

Before you plot anything

Fix periodic boundary crossings before RMSD, radius of gyration, or SASA. Drop the first 5–10 ns. A flat RMSD, radius of gyration, and SASA is the stability check this note uses. PCA and a free-energy landscape are the next look at slow motions. Those analysis commands are a separate post.

item.title: Molecular Simulation in Drug Discovery: A Strategic Guide to Core Methods
item.description:
The method has to match the question. Quantum mechanics can describe a bond breaking in an active site. It cannot watch a vesicle form. Dissipative particle dynamics can. This note places the usual drug-discovery methods on that scale and says what each one is for.

Quantum mechanics

QM solves the electronic problem. In a discovery project that means reactivity, an enzymatic mechanism, a transition state, partial charges for a force field, or a metal and a covalent ligand. The cost confines it to a small region. QM/MM keeps that region quantum and treats the rest of the protein classically.

Molecular dynamics

MD integrates Newton’s equations and returns a trajectory: protein motion, ligand binding, solvent, and stability. That is the usual check on a docked pose, an induced-fit hypothesis, or a binding free energy.

Sampling is the limit. A trajectory sits in the basin where it started. Metadynamics, accelerated MD, and replica-exchange MD are the enhanced-sampling routes named here. They still need a force field and, for most binding questions, an explicit solvent.

Coarse-grained MD

CGMD groups atoms into beads. The energy surface gets smoother and the system can be a membrane, a vesicle, or a nanoparticle. Drug-delivery formulations and lipid rafts sit at this scale. The result is qualitative or semi-quantitative. It is not an atomistic binding pose.

Monte Carlo

Monte Carlo samples configurations by probability instead of integrating time. Use it for conformers, side chains, and free-energy estimates inside docking workflows.

Grand canonical Monte Carlo also inserts and deletes molecules, including water. That is a way to find hydration sites and binding hotspots during lead optimization.

Brownian dynamics

BD drops inertia and keeps diffusion under thermal noise. The timescale is longer than MD, and the structural detail is thinner. The drug-discovery use is the encounter: an association rate constant, kon, or diffusion in a crowded compartment. It complements atomistic MD. It does not replace it.

Langevin dynamics

Langevin dynamics is MD plus friction and a random force. That combination holds the temperature and stands in for solvent damping, which is why it shows up with implicit solvent and as a simple thermostat. It can speed equilibration of a ligand or a conformational change. It is still a particle simulation, not a mesoscale one.

Dissipative particle dynamics

DPD is built for soft matter: polymers, lipids, surfactants. Particles are coarse-grained, and the dissipative and random forces are chosen so that momentum is conserved. That keeps hydrodynamics, so the method can show flow, self-assembly, encapsulation, and release. Formulation and nanomedicine are the applications in this note.

Hybrids

QM/MM is the hybrid already named above. Across scales, the same project can hand a ligand from BD to MD, or rebuild a coarse-grained configuration in atomistic detail. The sequence in the figure is one reading of that idea: BD for the encounter, MD for the pose, QM for the interaction energy. Each step answers a different question. None of them inherits the error bars of the previous one.

What to take from the list

Pick the coarsest method that still contains the physics you will claim. Electrons, a trajectory, a membrane, a water site, an on-rate, and a formulation are six different claims. The hardware is improving. The matching problem stays.

item.title: Understanding Molecular Dynamics Simulations
item.description:
Molecular dynamics does not search for a single best structure. It takes the structure you give it and asks what that structure does next.

You start with positions, velocities, and masses. A force field turns the current arrangement of atoms into forces. A short step, a few femtoseconds, uses those forces to update the positions and velocities. Then you do it again. The record of those updates is the trajectory.

What the step is doing

The force on an atom depends on the other atoms within range of the model: bonded terms for the bonds, angles, and dihedrals it belongs to, and nonbonded terms for electrostatics and van der Waals contacts. The force field is that model. It is an approximation with parameters, not a direct evaluation of the electronic Schrödinger equation.

The step has to be short because the forces are recomputed from the new geometry. A few femtoseconds is the usual scale, so that the fastest vibrations are not skipped. A nanosecond of simulation is therefore on the order of a million such updates. Nothing in the method jumps the system to a preferred pose. If a ligand moves, it moves because the accumulated steps carried it there.

What people use it for

In structural biology the interesting objects are already moving: side chains, loops, domains, and ligands. A crystal or cryo-EM structure is one configuration. The trajectory is a sample of configurations around and away from that start. Binding, conformational change, and contacts between molecules are read from that sample, which is why a single pretty frame from the run is a weak result.

The same loop is used in materials work. Polymers, ceramics, and metals are sets of particles with a force field appropriate to that material. Mechanical response, stability, and the effect of changing the conditions are again questions about the trajectory.

Two practical strengths follow from the setup. The system can contain many particles, so a protein of thousands of atoms is a normal target rather than a special case. The conditions are inputs. Temperature, pressure, and composition can be changed, and the comparison between two trajectories is often the actual experiment.

What comes out

The raw output is the trajectory: positions, and usually velocities and energies, along the time axis. Almost every figure in a paper is a reduction of that record.

Where the method stops

Two limits dominate.

The forces are only as faithful as the force field. A missing interaction, or a bad parameter, is integrated with the same confidence as a good one. The trajectory will not announce that the potential was wrong.

The other limit is cost. Each step looks at a large number of pairs, and interesting motions can require an enormous number of steps. Hardware and better algorithms have made routine protein–ligand runs accessible. They have not removed the gap between a femtosecond step and a slow biological event. How long a given question actually needs is a separate decision. The are the companion to this note.

Bottom line

An MD simulation is a loop. Configuration, forces, a femtosecond update, and a growing trajectory. Structural biology and materials work use that loop because the experiment they want is about motion under stated conditions. The interpretation lives in the reductions of the trajectory, and it inherits both the force field and the length of the run.

item.title: How Long Should Molecular Dynamics Simulations Run? A Practical Guide
item.description:
A protein–ligand simulation is long enough when the motion you care about has had time to happen, and the traces you are willing to trust have stopped drifting.

There is no single correct length. The ranges below are the ones that have proved useful for common questions. They are starting points. The trajectory, not the number you typed into the input file, tells you whether to stop.

Match the length to the event

Several windows have become usual for protein–ligand work, from published practice and from running these systems:

  • 50–100 nanoseconds. Often enough to judge initial binding stability, particularly with a small, rigid ligand and a relatively stable protein.
  • 100–200 nanoseconds. Room for ligand flexibility, side-chain reorganization, or early conformational change inside the pocket.
  • 200–500 nanoseconds. Slower events: partial unbinding, induced fit, or a shift at the domain level.
  • 500 nanoseconds to 1 microsecond, or longer. Long-timescale processes: allosteric communication, full ligand unbinding, or a global rearrangement of the protein.

These are guidelines. The required time moves with the system and with the question. A short run can be the right experiment when the question is whether a docked pose survives relaxation. It is the wrong experiment when the question is how the ligand leaves.

Convergence is the stopping rule

Convergence here means that the structural and energetic quantities you intend to interpret have settled. A long simulation that is still drifting does not become trustworthy because it is long. A short one that has plateaued on the observables you care about can be enough for that question.

Five checks cover the usual protein–ligand case.

  1. Root-mean-square deviation (RMSD). Deviation of the chosen atoms, often the protein backbone, from a reference over time. A plateau suggests that this part of the structure has stopped walking away from the reference. An RMSD that is still climbing means the rearrangement is not finished.
  2. Root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF). Flexibility per residue across the run. Once the trajectory is stable, RMSF profiles from successive windows look alike. A window that redraws the profile is a sign you have not settled.
  3. Energy. Total, potential, and kinetic energy. A system at equilibrium should not show a long drift. Sharp, persistent swings are a sign the equilibration was not long enough, or that something in the setup is wrong.
  4. Secondary structure. For a folded protein, helices and sheets that keep their assignment are a useful stability check. Assignments that keep flipping after the start of the production run are a reason to extend it.
  5. Interaction fingerprints. Hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, stacking, and the other contacts you claim as the binding pose. A pose is hard to defend when those contacts appear and vanish from one slice of the trajectory to the next.

An illustrative scenario

Imagine a complex whose RMSD rises over the first 50 nanoseconds while the pose settles, then levels off near 100 nanoseconds. Over that same later window the interaction fingerprint stops changing and the total energy no longer drifts. For a question about pose stability, extending the run may add little.

The opposite pattern is also common. The ligand keeps sliding in the pocket, or a domain keeps moving in one direction. That trajectory is asking for more time, or for an enhanced-sampling method aimed at the slow coordinate. Adding nanoseconds at random is a weaker response than naming the motion that has not converged.

What pushes the length up or down

  • Size and flexibility. A larger or more flexible protein has more conformational space to cross.
  • The ligand. Many rotatable bonds mean many poses. The dominant one may not be the pose you started from, and it may take longer to identify.
  • The question. Pose checking and a mechanism of unbinding are different experiments.
  • Replicates. Several independent runs often say more than one very long trajectory. A single run can look converged and still be stuck in the basin where it started.
  • The checks above. Decide in advance which observables would make you stop, and compute them before you interpret the pose.

Bottom line

For many protein–ligand questions about pose stability and interaction patterns, 50 to 200 nanoseconds is the window where those traces become readable. Unbinding, allosteric modulation, and large conformational change often need longer, sometimes past a microsecond.

Length is not a badge. A conclusion about a binding mode needs the traces that support it to have settled. If they have not, the honest result is that the simulation has not answered the question yet.
